## Appendix A Generalized Entropy on the Brane

In sections 2.3 and 2.4, we introduced intrinsic gravitational terms to the brane action. Following [22],4949 49 See also [20, 23, 29, 26, 25]. we assumed that these terms contribute to the generalized entropy, e.g., see eq. (3) or (68). In this appendix, we present a extended version of an argument in [46], which will support this assumption and our formula for generalized entropy.

As in the main text, we begin with a $d$ -dimensional holographic CFT on $R\times S^{d-1}$ with a conformal defect on the equator of the sphere, sweeping out $R\times S^{d-2}$ . On a fixed time-slice, we choose an entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ which divides the sphere into two equal halves along a maximal $S^{d-2}$ which lies orthogonal to the conformal defect. Now we wish to determine the entanglement entropy between the two halves of the system, as sketched in figure 14. Recall that with the geometric approach [138], we must evaluate the partition function on a (Euclidean) background geometry with an infinitesimal conical defect. In order to construct a symmetric geometry where introducing such a defect is well-defined, we perform a Wick rotation on the boundary time (i.e., $t_{\textrm{\tiny E}}=it$ ) and then conformally transform the Euclidean background metric to a round $S^{d}$ with the conformal defect lying on a maximal $S^{d-1}$ on this background. Now $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ remains a maximal $S^{d-2}$ which runs orthogonal to the defect and pierces the latter on a $S^{d-3}$ . With this construction, there is a rotational symmetry in the two dimensions orthogonal to $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ . To evaluate the corresponding entanglement entropy, we construct $\mathcal{M}_{1-\epsilon}$ , the ‘ $n$ -fold cover’ with $n=1-\epsilon$ , by introducing an infinitesimal conical defect at $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ . The entanglement entropy is then given by

$$ S=\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\left(\frac{\partial\ }{\partial\epsilon}+1\right)\log Z_{1-\epsilon}\,, $$

where $Z_{1-\epsilon}$ is the partition function of the holographic CFT on the covering space $\mathcal{M}_{1-\epsilon}$ . Of course, the latter has a dual description in terms of the bulk gravity, and using the usual saddle point approximation, eq. (126) becomes [46]

$$ S=-\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\Big(\frac{\partial}{\partial\epsilon}+1\Big)I_{E,1-\epsilon}\,, $$

where $I_{E,1-\epsilon}$ is the Euclidean bulk action evaluated on the appropriate dual solution.

*Figure 14: A timeslice of our $d$ -dimensional CFT setup with entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ and an equatorial conformal defect (the green line). In the right panel, one dimension is suppressed relative to the left panel.*

Setting $n=1$ for a moment, the bulk dual of $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ is simply the Euclidean version of the geometry constructed in section 2.1, which we denote $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1}$ . Recall the boundary geometry is $S^{d}$ and the conformal defect runs around a maximal $S^{d-1}$ . In the bulk, the geometry is locally EAdSd+1 everywhere away from the brane, and the brane has a EAdSd geometry which extends out to the conformal defect at the asymptotic boundary and with the curvature scale given by eq. (16) – see figure 15. Now the entangling surface $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ on the asymptotic AdS boundary is the boundary of an extremal surface $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ in the bulk, which runs straight across the bulk solution and has a EAdSd-1 geometry with curvature scale $L$ . This surface pierces the brane at a right angle and the intersection, another extremal surface $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , has the geometry of a EAdSd-2 with curvature scale $\ell_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ – see figure 15. Now because of the symmetry of this configuration, the rotational symmetry about the entangling surface in the boundary extends to a rotational symmetry about $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ in the bulk. Hence we can calculate the entanglement entropy with the same geometric approach as we applied in the boundary. That is, we construct $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1-\epsilon}$ , the $n$ -fold cover (with $n=1-\epsilon$ ) of the bulk solution with a infinitesimal conical defect at $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ and by extension, at $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ on the brane.

*Figure 15: A cross-section of the Euclidean geometry $\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}_{1}$ . The orange semicircle and its complement along a time slice represent the orange shaded region of figure 14 and its complement. The rotation that keeps $\Sigma_{\textrm{\tiny CFT}}$ fixed represents euclidean time. An infinitesimal conical defect $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ runs through the bulk and intersects the brane at $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ .*

That is, the angle around $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ runs through a range $2\pi(1-\epsilon)$ . Now [139, 140] developed a description of such conical defects in which the singular geometry is replaced by a ‘regulator’ geometry where the region around the conical singularity is smoothed out. Applying their key result, we can write the bulk Riemann tensor as a “smooth” contribution away from $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , the conical defect, and a singular order $\epsilon$ contribution at $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ ,5050 50 This order $\epsilon$ contribution is universal, whereas the details of the regulator come into play at order $\epsilon^{2}$ and higher.

$$ ^{(\epsilon)}R^{ab}{}_{cd}=R^{ab}{}_{cd}+2\pi\epsilon\,{\varepsilon}^{ab}{\varepsilon}_{cd}\,\delta_{\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}\,, $$

where ${\varepsilon}_{ab}$ is the Euclidean volume form in the two-dimensional transverse space to $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , and $R^{ab}{}_{cd}$ is the “smooth” curvature piece. The $\delta_{\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}$ is a two-dimensional delta function defined in [46]. The conical singularity intersects the brane at $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ and so we have a similar decomposition for the Riemann tensor on the brane,

$$ ^{(\epsilon)}\tilde{R}^{ij}{}_{k\ell}=\tilde{R}^{ij}{}_{k\ell}+2\pi\epsilon\,\tilde{\varepsilon}^{ij}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{k\ell}\,\delta_{\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}\,. $$

Now recall that our aim is to evaluate the Euclidean action in eq. (127). This action is the sum of the Euclidean versions5151 51 Note that the difference in signs in going between Minkowski and Euclidean signatures [46]. of the bulk and brane actions in eqs. (4) and (49) (or perhaps eq. (41) for $d=2$ ), as well as the associated boundary terms. Equipped with eqs. (128) and (129), it can be shown that in the limit of small $\epsilon$ that the Euclidean action can be expanded as

$$ \displaystyle I_{E,1-\epsilon} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1-\epsilon)I_{E,1}+\int_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}\!\!d^{d+1}x\sqrt{g}\,2\pi\epsilon{\varepsilon}^{ab}{\varepsilon}_{cd}\,\delta_{\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{\tiny E,bulk}}}{\partial R^{ab}{}_{cd}} \displaystyle\qquad+\int_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}\!\!\!\!d^{d}x\sqrt{\tilde{g}}\,2\pi\epsilon\tilde{\varepsilon}^{ij}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{k\ell}\,\delta_{\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{\tiny E,brane}}}{\partial\tilde{R}^{ij}{}_{k\ell}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\,. $$

Noting the symmetry of our configuration, i.e., the curvatures are constant everywhere along the surfaces $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , we then find the entropy in eq. (127) is given by

$$ S=-2\pi\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{\tiny E,bulk}}}{\partial R^{ab}{}_{cd}}{\varepsilon}^{ab}{\varepsilon}_{cd}\int_{\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}d^{d-1}x\sqrt{h}-2\pi\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\textrm{\tiny E,brane}}}{\partial\tilde{R}^{ij}{}_{k\ell}}\tilde{\varepsilon}^{ij}\tilde{\varepsilon}_{k\ell}\int_{\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}}d^{d-2}x\sqrt{h^{\prime}}\,, $$

where $h$ and $h^{\prime}$ are the induced metrics along the $\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ and $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ , respectively. Hence we see that there is a contribution of the Wald entropy from both the bulk action and the brane action. Further, let us note that various signs appear upon analytically continuing back to Lorentzian spacetime, i.e., in the Lagrangian and the transverse volume form [46].

For the case where the Einstein-Hilbert action appears both in the bulk and on the brane, as in eqs. (4) and (49), we find the formula for the generalized entropy (132) becomes

$$ S=\frac{A(\Sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}+\frac{A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\,, $$

as given in equation (68). The present derivation only applies to special symmetric configuration, as in [46]. The symmetry of this configuration preculdes finding any extrinsic curvature terms in eq. (132), as would be expected for the Dong entropy [101]. We note however that no such terms would correct eq. (133) for the generalized entropy coming from the Einstein-Hilbert term. It would, of course, be interesting to extend our derivation to more general configurations involving bulk DGP branes, along the lines of [10] or [111].

## Appendix B RT Bubbles

In this appendix, we consider a simple but surprising class of RT surfaces. In particular, we show below that there are closed extremal surfaces with the topology of a sphere, i.e., $S^{d-1}$ in the locally AdSd+1 bulk geometry. In empty AdS space, one could consider such spherical surfaces, but their area would be extremized when they collapse to zero size. In the present case, we will show that in certain situations, the spherical RT surfaces can be supported at finite size by the brane. To illustrate the situation, we continue with the special case of $d=3$ as in section 4.4, and afterwards comment on the situation with general $d$ .

*Figure 16: An RT ‘bubble’ on the brane: even for the vacuum, when $G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}<0$ the competing bulk and brane area terms can lead to a stable extremal surface, which is homologous to the entire time slice for the boundary CFT. The entanglement wedge then corresponds to the shaded red region. Since the two sides of the brane are glued together, the RT surface has the topology of $S^{d-1}$ .*

Consider the geometry illustrated in figure 16. On either side of the brane, we have a disk satisfying $\zeta=$ constant, i.e., satisfying eq. (106) with $P_{0}=0$ . Hence locally these surfaces extremize the entropy functional (105) in the bulk. However, rather than extending out to the asymptotic boundary, as shown in the figure, the two disks intersect the brane and meet at some radius $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Hence this RT surface has the topology of a sphere and we use the nomenclature ‘bubble’ to describe these surfaces. For $d=3$ , the generalised entropy (68) of this bubble is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}} \displaystyle=\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\left(\sqrt{1+P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}-1+\lambda_{b}\,P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}\right)+2\,\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}} $$

with $\lambda_{b}$ defined in eq. (53). We have also included the topological term introduced in eq. (111). Of course, since these surfaces never reach the asymptotic boundary, this quantity is finite, i.e., there are no UV divergences in eq. (134).

Extremizing eq. (134) with respect to the radius of the bubble, we find

$$ \partial_{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}=0\qquad\implies\qquad\frac{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}{\sqrt{1+P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}}}=-\lambda_{b}=-\frac{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}{2L\,G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}}\,. $$

Now recall that we will always have $G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}>0$ , but considered the possibility of $G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ becoming negative in section 4.4. Let us first consider the case $\lambda_{b}\geq 0$ , which implies $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}\geq 0$ . In this case, we can not satisfy eq. (135), since both the bulk and brane contributions to the generalised entropy (134) are positive and monotonically increasing functions of $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Therefore the minimum lies at $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=0$ , i.e., where the bubble collapses to zero size – see figure (17).

Of course, the more interesting scenario is when $\lambda_{b}$ , and hence $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ , are negative. Then eq. (135) has the solution

$$ \displaystyle P_{\textrm{\tiny B,0}}=-\frac{\lambda_{b}}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{b}^{2}}}\,, $$

for which the generalized entropy (134) becomes

$$ \displaystyle S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}=\frac{\pi L^{2}}{G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\left(\sqrt{1-\lambda_{b}^{2}}-1\right)+2\,\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}. $$

We note that these expressions are only sensible for $-1<\lambda_{b}<0$ . In fact, for $\lambda_{b}<-1$ , there is no minimum for the generalized entropy (134), i.e., there is no solution for eq. (135), and rather $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ runs off to infinity – see figure (17). This is, perhaps, not so surprising since we can see from eq. (54) that this regime is pathological, with the graviton localized on the brane becoming a ghost.

Therefore we only consider the regime $-1<\lambda_{b}<0$ where eqs. (136) and (137) apply. As illustrated in figure (17), eq. (136) is indeed the global minimum of the generalized entropy (134). We might note that the sum of the bulk and brane terms in eq. (137) is negative. That is, the combined contributions of the two area terms in eq. (68) is in fact negative! Hence we only get a sensible (i.e., positive) result for the generalized entropy (134) with the inclusion of the topological term (111) and with $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}$ sufficiently positive, which was also favoured in section 4.4.

For $\lambda_{b}<-1$ , there is no global minimum, signalling an instability of the system. Further note that as $P_{0}$ approaches zero, $S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}\to\pi L^{2}/G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}$ since we have set $\lambda_{\textrm{\tiny GB}}=\pi L^{2}/(2G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}})$ .*

Now, we observe that for large $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , the leading contribution in eq. (138) takes the expected form

$$ S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}\simeq\frac{A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}+\cdots\qquad{\rm where}\ \ \ \frac{A(\sigma_{\mathbf{R}})}{4G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}}=\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{2(d-2)G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,(1+\lambda_{b})\,P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{d-2}\,, $$

again using eq. (53). Hence, there is a large penalty for having the RT surface meet the brane at a large radius $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , which will tend to push the intersection $\sigma_{\mathbf{R}}$ to smaller radii. However, for small $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ , the bulk contribution to $S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}$ grows like the volume, i.e., it is proportional to $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{d-1}$ . Hence in this regime, the brane contribution dominates since it is proportional to $\lambda_{b}P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{d-2}$ , and for $\lambda_{b}<0$ , this term will favour larger values of $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ . Hence for the interesting case of $\lambda_{b}<0$ , we can expect that the generalized entropy for general $d$ is extremized at some finite value of $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}$ of order $-\lambda_{b}$ , just as we found for $d=3$ . Of course, the denominator in eq. (136) is also important for $\lambda_{b}$ close to $-1$ , but this can not be seen with this simple qualitative analysis. Now, in fact, the extremality condition can in fact be solved exactly for any $d$ . One finds

$$ \partial_{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}=\frac{L^{d-1}\,\Omega_{d-2}}{2G_{\textrm{\tiny bulk}}}\,P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{d-3}\left(\frac{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}}{\sqrt{P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}^{2}+1}}+\lambda_{b}\right)=0\,. $$

Of course, for $\lambda_{b}\geq 0$ , the only solution is $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=0$ , i.e., the bubble collapses to zero size, as expected. However, for $\lambda_{b}<0$ , the minimum is given by $P_{\textrm{\tiny B}}=P_{\textrm{\tiny B,0}}$ , precisely the same critical radius as in eq. (136). Substituting this critical radius into the generalized entropy (138) does not yield any simplifications, however the result is easily evaluated numerically as a function of $\lambda_{b}$ . Of course, the generalized entropy (138) is negative at this minimum and so one would really need to add a topological term to the gravitational theory, either in the bulk or on the brane, to produce a sensible entropy, as we did for the $d=3$ example.

### Wormholes and Cutoffs

The appearance of these extremal bubbles is quite unusual, of course. Since they are homologous to the entire boundary, this suggests that the ground state of the dual boundary system has an entropy by the standard RT prescription. The bulk construction makes clear that it is the conformal defect which introduces this large degeneracy of ground states.5252 52 As we see in figure 17, entropy associated with the zero-size bubble is nonvanishing and higher than that of the stable finite-size bubble due to the topological contribution. However, we note that it may be that the correct RT prescription is to choose ‘empty surface’ in this case, giving zero entropy.

We should note, however, that the evaluation of this ground state entropy presented above is incomplete. In particular, there is a ‘zero mode’ associated with these bubbles which allows them to be translated along the brane. Recall that while the empty AdSd+1 geometry has an $SO(2,d)$ isometry (reflecting the conformal symmetry group of the boundary CFT), the backreacted brane geometry preserves an $SO(2,d-1)$ subgroup of these symmetries. Now our construction places the center of the bubbles at $P=0$ , however, by acting with these symmetries, we can position the center anywhere on the brane. Further recall that one arrives at the RT prescription by evaluating (a particular limit of) a saddlepoint in the gravitational path integral [10]. Hence we have discovered that there is a zero mode associated with the saddlepoints connected to the bubbles. Hence the integral over this zero mode would add a contribution to the entropy proportional to the logarithm of the (regulated) brane volume. It is interesting to speculate that this contribution may lift the negative value for $S_{\textrm{\tiny gen}}(P_{\textrm{\tiny B,0}})$ to some positive entropy.

An essential feature required for the appearance of these bubbles was that the gravitational coupling associated with the DGP term (49) was negative, i.e., $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}<0$ . While this may seem unusual, let us note that integrating out quantum fields on the brane can produce either a positive or negative shift in Newton’s constant. In particular, the shift is found to be negative for a $U(1)$ gauge field when $d<8$ [108, 109]. With the connection between the renormalization of Newton’s constant and the area law contribution in entanglement entropy [138, 141], this negative renormalization generates a puzzle which, however, was finally resolved in terms of edge modes in [142, 143]. There is a similar negative renormaliation for non-minimally coupled scalars [108], for which the resolution of the associated puzzle appears in [18]. However, we should add that if we imagine $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}<0$ is induced by additional quantum fields on the brane, then our entanglement entropy calculations are incomplete as they do not fully include the contributions of these extra fields. Hence our perspective here is to simply view the DGP term as a counterterm as would appear in the usual quantization of gravity on the brane, and in this context, the sign of $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ is not proscribed but rather is chosen as needed to produce the ‘observed’ value of $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny eff}}$ .

Another remark in this vein is that the bubble solutions appear as soon as $1/G_{\textrm{\tiny brane}}$ is negative, i.e., these solutions (136) exist for very small values of $\lambda_{b}$ as long as $\lambda_{b}<0$ . However, it is important to recall that the short distance cutoff is given by eq. (62) in this regime. Hence combining eqs. (101) and (136), the areal size of the bubbles becomes

$$ LP_{\textrm{\tiny B,0}}=\frac{|\lambda_{b}|\,L}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{b}^{2}}}\simeq\frac{|\lambda_{b}|}{\sqrt{1+|\lambda_{b}|}}\,\tilde{\delta}\,. $$

where we have substituted eq. (58) in the second expression. This expression approaches the maximum size $\tilde{\delta}/\sqrt{2}$ as $\lambda_{b}\to-1$ . That is, the radius of bubbles is always smaller than the cutoff scale $\tilde{\delta}$ on the brane! Therefore, these solutions are not reliable in the regime where Einstein gravity gives a good description of the brane. On the other hand, our calculations in this appendix involved evaluating RT surfaces in the bulk, i.e., they only depended on bulk perspective. Further, for $|\lambda_{b}|\gtrsim 1/\sqrt{2}$ , the corresponding RT surfaces grow much larger than the bulk AdS scale, and so would be seen as valid solutions. However, one may ask if there are physical constraints which will not allow us to realize theories with $\lambda_{b}$ which are that negative and so prevent us from considering scenarios where these bubbles have a macroscopic size.

We close here with two final remarks: These bubbles are a remnant of replica wormholes in the limit $n\to 1$ [26, 32]. In the discussion section, we explore if there are any lessons that they may hold for the new discussions of baby universes and ensembles [33]. Another comment is that the bubble surfaces produce an interesting entanglement wedge, which extends to a band covering a finite time interval on the boundary. Of course, this is reminiscent of the holographic construction of differential entropy [144, 145, 146, 147, 148], which can be used to evaluate the area of closed surfaces in the bulk. It would be interesting to examine these connections further.
